title: Fading Support
author: Jamie Lee Clark
source: DistillED by Jamie Lee Clark, July 30, 2026
summary: This edition of DistillED explains fading support — the deliberate, staged removal of scaffolds as students become more competent — as the missing half of scaffolding. The clearest evidence comes from backward fading research by Renkl and Atkinson: removing the end of a worked example first produces stronger outcomes than removing the beginning, contrary to teacher instinct. Fading sits within the Gradual Release of Responsibility framework but is more precise than 'I do, we do, you do' — it is a responsive withdrawal calibrated to evidence of student competence. Traditional approaches that jump from complete worked examples to independent practice create an 'ignored impasse' problem where students recognize difficulty and skip on without resolving it. Backward fading improved performance on both familiar and transfer tasks without extra learning time, making it a high-leverage technique for any teacher who currently provides scaffolds.
points: Fading support is the missing half of scaffolding — without a planned withdrawal, temporary support quietly becomes permanent.
Backward fading (removing the end of a worked example first) outperforms forward fading and is the opposite of what most teachers do instinctively.
The traditional jump from full worked example to independent problem creates an 'ignored impasse' — students get stuck and move on without resolving the difficulty.
Backward fading improved performance on both familiar problems and unfamiliar transfer problems without requiring additional learning time.
Fading should be driven by evidence of student competence, not a fixed timetable — the pace of withdrawal must respond to what students can actually do.
quotes: Fading is the missing half of scaffolding — it is not a separate idea, but the part of the sequence that turns temporary support into independent capability.
